en: A Brief Exposition of the General Meaning of Each Fascicle of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddhas of the Great Vaipulya,
composed by Li Tongxuan of Beijing.

Volume One, First Fascicle: The First Assembly at the Site of Enlightenment (*Bodhimaṇḍa*). Six chapters of the sutra are spoken herein, up to Volume Five. Chapter One: "The Sublime Array of the World-Protectors. The Buddha attained enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha and preached the Dharma within the Site of Enlightenment.
Because they practiced together with the Buddha in past kalpas, he has caused this ocean-like assembly to gather.
In the second fascicle, regarding the various species of animals and the devas of the upper realms, each has attained partial realization and liberation within the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruition.
In the third fascicle: the four kings, the eight classes [of spirits], and various other deities all used exquisite words of invitation to chant and praise the inconceivable Dharma.
In the fourth fascicle: Myriad forms and appearances, divided into a thousand classes, each proclaiming the gateways to liberation and praising the Tathāgata’s virtues in verse.

Fifth Fascicle. Through the inconceivable power of the Tathāgata, all the bodhisattvas rose from their seats; auspicious omens flowed through heaven and earth, and the ocean-like assembly made offerings to the boundless Buddhas.

Fascicle Six, Chapter Two: The Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata. The great assembly collectively offered their mindful request, and the Tathāgata responded by manifesting signs. Through light and sound, he summoned those with karmic affinity, and a new multitude from the ten directions gathered like clouds.

Volume Seven, Chapter Three: The Samādhi of Samantabhadra; Chapter Four: The Formation of Worlds. In this chapter, Samantabhadra enters the *kośa-garbha-samādhi*. Through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s holy power, he arises from meditative absorption and expounds the Dharma-gate of the Ten Seas, extensively elucidating the establishment of worlds.

In the eighth fascicle: The wind-wheel supports the great waters; the great ocean surges with lotuses; fragrant rivers are arranged throughout the world-systems (*kṣetra-vyuha*); and worlds are layered within the central sea.
Volume Nine, Chapter Five: The Accomplishment of Worlds and the Flower Treasury World. To the right, ten oceans spiral in succession, connecting one another in layers upon layers of interlacing.
Like a net of celestial jewels.

Volume Ten through Volume Eleven. Chapter Six: Vairocana. Regarding the ocean of lands governed therein, extending straight to the Flower Treasury Adornment equal to the Dharmadhātu bounded by the Cakravāḍa mountains, this section presents the fruition to encourage all beings to develop faith and joy.

Volume Eleven. Vairocana, in a past eon, was once the Prince Majestic Light (*Vaiśvānara-tejas*); he made offerings to as many Tathāgatas as there are atoms in ten Mount Sumerus, causing them to attain the ocean of fruits of ten Lotus Treasury Worlds.

The Twelfth Fascicle. The Second Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance. Six Chapters of the Sūtra are Expounded. Chapter Seven: The Names of the Buddhas; Chapter Eight: The Four Noble Truths. The names of the Tathāgatas are manifold, as they are adapted to the diverse capacities of sentient beings.
The Four Noble Truths are established according to the circumstances of each region, so that all who hear the Dharma may attain realization.

Volume Thirteen, Chapter Nine: "The Chapter on Radiant Awakening"; Chapter Ten: "The Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into Clarification. In these sections, Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Navamukha inquire about ten kinds of profound mysteries; all serve to reveal the mutual integration of essence and characteristics, thereby shattering the doubts and attachments of all sentient beings.

Volume Fourteen. Chapter Eleven: Purifying Conduct; Chapter Twelve: Worthy Leader. Purifying conduct gives rise to boundless great vows; Mañjuśrī instructs on skillfully employing the mind; Worthy Leader manifests virtuous conduct; the verses reveal that faith possesses infinite great utility.
Fascicle Fifteen. In the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders," the Samādhi of the Light of the Hairs Illuminating Benefit employs metaphors to express the profound and mysterious ultimate meaning.
It praises the inconceivability of this sutra and exhorts its upholding; all Buddhas touch one’s head and rejoice in accordance.

Volume Sixteen, Volume Sixteen: The Third Assembly in the Palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Explaining Six Chapters. Chapter Thirteen: Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru; Chapter Fourteen: Verses of Praise; Chapter Fifteen: The Ten Abodes. The "Verses on Mount Sumeru" clarifies that the Buddha’s virtues are not left behind as he ascends to heaven;
the "Explanation of the Gates of the Ten Abodes" distinguishes the essential purpose of the Bodhisattvas’ entry into their respective stages.

Volume Seventeen. Chapter Sixteen: The Holy Life (*Brahmacarya*); Chapter Seventeen: The Merit of the Initial Resolve (*Prathamacittotpāda*). The holy life brings about the realization that objects are empty and quiescent, so that one does not give rise to a dualistic mind.
The merit manifested by the initial resolve is boundless; with the very first thought, one attains perfect awakening.

Volume Eighteen. Chapter Eighteen: The Exposition on Clarifying the Dharma. This chapter explains that by clarifying the Dharma, one proclaims the non-interruption of the Triple Gem, whereby those below may find peace and happiness among humans and devas;
through the ten practices and ten kinds of dharma-gates, those above seek the stages of spiritual advancement.

Volume Nineteen. The Fourth Assembly in the Palace of the Yāma Heaven. Exposition of the Sūtra in Four Chapters. Chapter Nineteen: Ascending to the Palace of the Yāma Heaven; Chapter Twenty: Verses of Praise; Chapter Twenty-one: The Ten Practices. The verses of praise from the Yāma Heaven manifest the inexhaustibility of the Buddha’s virtues, while simultaneously revealing the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices and extensively discussing the skillful mastery of the Bodhisattvas.
Volume Twenty. Chapter Twenty: The Ten Practices. This is the fourth section on the True Nature of Non-attachment and others, clarifying the two gates of self-benefit and benefiting others.
The direct realizations since the beginning are inconceivable; these verses are again included here to honor the virtues of the predecessors.

Volume Twenty-One. The Twenty-first Volume: The Twenty Tenth, the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries. These twenty inexhaustible treasuries are followed by all Buddhas of the three periods of time; they do not pertain solely to the meaning of the dharma-gate of the ten practices, but also transcend the superior progress of dedication.

Volume Twenty-Two, Fifth Assembly of the Tuṣita Heaven Palace, Exposition of the Sūtra in Three Sections; Chapter Twenty-Three: Ascending to the Tuṣita Heaven Palace—The Transformation Master Responds to Conditions.
Beholding the Buddha’s divine radiance, the celestial kings attained benefit.

In the twenty-third fascicle, the twenty-fourth chapter, "Verses of Praise," at the beginning of the tenth dedication of the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, the boundless compassion and wisdom of the Bodhisattva are revealed as they rescue sentient beings from suffering throughout long kalpas. The section on the Celestial King Contented with What He Has offers verses of praise.
Volume Twenty-four through Volume Thirty-three. Chapter Twenty-five: The Ten Dedications. "Unbreakable Firm Resolve" is the dharma-gate that is equal to all Buddhas.
The practices and vows encompass all things, turning the Sugata toward the appropriate time and place.
In the twenty-fifth fascicle, the twenty-fifth fascicle: good causes contain their fruits, establishing the name of the inexhaustible treasury;
when the roots of goodness unite with the Truth, they are identical to the inexhaustibility of the nature of Suchness.

Volume Twenty-Six. From the giving of chariots and horses up to the giving of one's own body, this section consists of ten long passages concerning great causes, wherein both internal and external things are entirely renounced.

In the twenty-seventh fascicle: The Bodhisattva relinquished his topknot together with its skin, even down to saving those whose forms were but remnants; adorning his body with the ten thousand practices, he perfected the ten marks of a Great Man.

In the twenty-eighth fascicle, from its beginning to its end, one beholds the sixty gates of great giving manifested by the Buddha’s appearance; the three preceding fascicles collectively encompass the long discourse on steadfast dedication.
In the twenty-ninth fascicle: The sentient beings whom one follows are signless, yet one can accord with their mental activities.
Furthermore, like the two kinds of giving that extensively fill incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya*), one vows to be fully endowed with both wealth and the Dharma.
The thirtieth fascicle: The virtue of the hundred gates is as one, like a string threading through beads.
Performing good deeds equal to space, they likewise share the same nature and characteristics, pervading all extensively.
In the thirty-first fascicle: By means of liberation from the fetters of formless delusions, one attains the name of "dedication.
Through the six kinds of subtle gates of wisdom, may one realize the virtues of Samantabhadra.

Volume Thirty-Two. Within a single body, one encompasses the entire dharma-realm; at the tip of a hair, one gathers all myriad phenomena. By turning back these roots of goodness that are equal to the dharma-realm, one accomplishes the great function of Samantabhadra throughout the dust-motes and lands of the universe.

In the thirty-third fascicle, both the primary and secondary fruits are adorned with countless jewels; this concludes the praise and exhortation for the fulfillment of the merit of cultivating the stage of Samantabhadra.

Volume Thirty-Four. The Sixth Assembly in the Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. One chapter of the sutra is spoken, continuing through Volume Thirty-Nine. Chapter Twenty-Six: The Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*). In the Mani-Jewel Palace of the Paranirmita-vaśavartins, the Dharma-gate of the Ten Stages is first opened.
After three additions and five requests, he finally set forth the characteristics of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
In the thirty-fifth fascicle, concerning the Bodhisattva of the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), he cultivates the dharma-gate of the ten wholesome actions in three clusters;
through the eight meditative concentrations and five supernormal powers, he gives rise to the blazing radiance of boundless, wondrous wisdom.
Volume Thirty-Six. The Flame of Wisdom that Realizes Capable Knowledge: A Dharma Gate for Progressing in the Factors of Enlightenment.
Relying upon the Śrāvaka’s contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, it reveals the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s superior stages (*bhūmi*).
Volume Thirty-Seven. The thirty-seventh volume: The manifestation of Prajñā and the tenfold contemplation of the dharma of dependent origination.
Having traveled for a long duration, one surpasses the preceding and succeeding stages at the seventh bhūmi.

In the thirty-eighth fascicle: Without realizing the principle of non-arising, one relies on the Buddha’s bridge of seven exhortations; with great compassion, he observes the ten kinds of dense forests of sentient beings, and with great wisdom, he flows forth as a Bodhisattva, employing eloquence to expound the Dharma.
Volume Thirty-Nine. Volume Thirty-Nine: The vast virtues of self and others, like clouds and rain, are in their minor aspects not equal to those of the Tathāgata.

Within this, causes and effects intermingle; many analogies and comparisons are used to measure what cannot be fathomed, such as the Heaven of the Third Dhyāna. The seventh assembly contains missing text.

Volume Forty. The fortieth volume contains the eighth assembly, the Reunion at Universal Radiance (*Samantābhāsā*), which expounds eleven chapters of the sutra, extending to Volume Forty-three. Chapter Twenty-seven, "The Ten Samādhis" (*Daśaniyama*): Since the ultimate fruit must necessarily arise from initial faith, the Dharma Hall was reconvened.
Samantabhadra, having received this command, proclaims it; he shall now definitively set forth the superior functions of the ten samādhis.

In the forty-first fascicle, the "Samādhi of Universally Abiding in All Lands," including the ten kinds of adornments, he speaks of the sovereign supernormal powers of Bodhisattvas, manifesting the inexhaustible merits of Samantabhadra.

Volume Forty-Two. The function of arising and entering the Samādhi of Differentiated Sovereignty has no other divisions; it surges forth from the four gates as a vast tide, and the mind’s flow of the four analytical knowledges expounds the teaching.

Volume Forty-Three. The forty-third volume: The Samādhi of the Unimpeded Great Wheel has the power to pervade the entire Dharma-realm; like the transformations of the King of the Celestial Multitudes, it is equal to Perfect Enlightenment and identical to Wondrous Enlightenment.
Fascicle Forty-Four. Chapter Twenty-Eight: The Ten Supernatural Powers; Chapter Twenty-Nine: The Ten Endurances. Expanding upon the sovereign eloquence, he elucidates the ten kinds of bodies.
The supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the Dharma are elucidated through both analogy and exposition, setting forth the characteristics of the ten patiences (*kṣānti*).

In the forty-fifth fascicle: the thirtieth chapter, "The Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*); the thirty-first chapter, "Life Span"; and the thirty-second chapter, "The Abodes of Bodhisattvas. The incalculable life spans manifest the inexhaustibility of the Buddha’s virtues;
the responsive manifestations according to various regions demonstrate the abodes of the bodhisattvas.

Scroll Forty-six, continuing to Scroll Forty-seven: Chapter Thirty-three, "The Inconceivable Dharma. The Great Assembly, harboring doubts and reflections, made their request, not yet knowing what the marks of virtue were like.
The Blue Lotus (Utpala) employs eloquent disputation to offer a reply in return, discussing the inconceivable fruits of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Throughout the forty-seventh fascicle, the vast Buddhist activities from beginning to end cultivate the gateway to liberation.
He erects the Dharma-banner of lofty and courageous strength and proclaims the far-reaching resonance of the perfect voice.

In the forty-eighth fascicle—specifically the thirty-fourth chapter, "The Ocean of Marks of the Tathāgata’s Ten Bodies," and the thirty-fifth chapter, "The Merit of the Radiance of the Minor Marks"—both the ocean of marks of the ten bodies and the radiance of the minor marks reveal that his virtuous functions are inconceivable, while his causes are profound and his fruits are far-reaching.
Fascicle Forty-nine. Chapter Thirty-six: The Conduct of Samantabhadra. A single delusion constitutes one million gates of obstruction.
The verses separately clarify the ten practices, interwoven yet unmixed.
Fascicle 50 through Fascicle 52: Chapter 37, "The Appearance of the Tathāgata. Regarding the appearance of the Tathāgata, there are many approaches through both Dharma teachings and parables.
The ten bodies are subsumed and harmonized; the single principle brings balance and illuminates all with clarity.
In the fifty-first fascicle, the eloquence of his speech pours forth the resonance of the perfect sound, responding to the hidden currents of the water of wise illumination.
Shattering the subtle dust to bring forth the Great Sūtra, and cleaving open the ordinary mind to manifest sagely wisdom.

In the fifty-second fascicle—fifty-second fascicle—the realms, practices, and the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and Nirvāṇa: to draw near to, see, or hear these is not in vain; it establishes the indestructible, adamantine seed of firmness.

Fascicle Fifty-three. In the ninth assembly of the Triple Array of Universal Radiance, one chapter of the sutra is expounded, continuing through fascicle fifty-nine: Chapter Thirty-eight, "Transcending the World," concerning how Bodhisattvas dwell in the world without being defiled—this is the "Chapter on Transcending the World."
The Cloud of Universal Wisdom appears to initiate the inquiry, while Samantabhadra pours forth his responses from his flask.

From the fifty-fourth fascicle, beginning with the ten kinds of consolation (*āśvāsa*) and extending to the gate of the Peerless Abode (*asama-vihāra*), more than three hundred long passages provide the responses corresponding to the characteristics of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*).
Fascicle Fifty-Five. Fascicle Fifty-Five: The ten kinds of impermanence are presented hereafter, followed by the gates of mastery (*vaśitā*) and so forth.
The purport within these is boundless, as it describes the preceding stage of dedication (*pariṇāmana*).

Fascicle Fifty-Six. At the beginning of this fifty-sixth fascicle, the titles list ten kinds of non-obstruction; extending through the manifest text of the Great Lion’s Roar, there are numerous dharma-gates that expand upon the virtues of the Ten Stages.

Fascicle Fifty-Seven. This fascicle fifty-seven treats the severance of the ten remaining habitual tendencies; it subsequently discusses the mind of further advancement (*viśeṣābhyudgata-citta*), comprising thirty-three sections in total that comprehensively clarify practices for leaving behind defilement (*vimala-carita*) and so forth.

Fascicle Fifty-Eight. Beginning from the Bodhisattva’s Pure Giving and extending down to the Ten Gates of Descent into Birth, the practices and vows therein are inexhaustible; this constitutes the aspect of fulfilling the retribution of causes and conditions.
Fascicle Fifty-nine. Fascicle Fifty-nine: The eight signs of descending into the mother’s womb, with verses exhorting one to practice;
the two thousand gates of conduct for single-minded renunciation; this constitutes the section on the completion of cultivation.

Volume Sixty, Chapter Sixty: The Tenth Assembly of the Multi-storied Hall at Jetavana. A single chapter of the sutra is spoken, continuing through Volume Eighty: The Thirty-ninth Chapter, "Entering the Dharma Realm. Without departing from the Jeta Grove, the Tathāgata enters the Lion’s Yawn Samādhi.
The Bodhisattvas behold the divine transformations of the Dharma-realm, while the Śrāvakas remain deaf and blind, unaware of them.

In the sixty-first fascicle, Samantabhadra is able to unfold the ten phrases, and the Tathāgata extends a single ray of light from his white tuft of hair; Mañjuśrī follows him southward, all of which manifests the fruit-virtues of the gates of meditative concentration.

Volume Sixty-Two. In this sixty-second volume, the Great Sage exhorts Sudhana to seek spiritual friends by traveling south; he visits Meghashiri and Samudrareṇu, who bestow upon him the Dharma-gate of "Abiding Well," which is profound, subtle, and unfathomable.
Volume Sixty-Three. Meeting Mṛkaṇḍa and the Householder Vimukta, they realize the wondrous gateway of the Revolving Dhāraṇī.
Later, they see the Bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja and behold the sublime phenomena manifested from the hairs of his body.

Volume Sixty-Four. Volume Sixty-Four: Paying homage to the friend of Śūnyatā-ghoṣa, he merely took his hand and traveled throughout the ten directions; he was exhorted to go to the Mountain of Knives of Jvalana-mukha and cast himself into a mass of fire to attain samādhi.

Fascicle Sixty-Five. From the maiden Maitrīcaryā at the beginning to the householder Prajñākūṭa at the end, these four spiritual friends all entrust their teachings to the Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices.

Fascicle Sixty-Six. The elder Baoji (Jewel-Crest) Puyan (Universal Eye), King Wuyandaiguang (Great Light of Insatiability), and the past causes of Buddhanamaskāra-asaṃhārya-kathā (The Unshakable One Who Speaks of Reverence for the Buddha); this Dharma-gate contains the profound meaning of both the adverse and the favorable.

Fascicle Sixty-Seven. Fascicle Sixty-Seven: The Universal Manifestation of the Forms of the Six Realms; the Dharma Gate of the Fivefold Method of the Incense Merchant; the Supreme Victor Using the Four *Kaṣāyas* to Deliver Beings; and the Lion Nun Sitting on Her Seat to Discourse on the Dharma.

Volume Sixty-Eight. Vāsuki and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahādeva, and the earth goddess Anantāvasthita, together with their virtuous friends, cultivate the dharma-gate of dedication (pariṇāmanā). Vāsana refers to the noble stage of the first bhūmi.
In the sixty-ninth fascicle: the night goddess Samantaguṇa teaches the gate of liberation known as "Wandering Steps";
the night goddess Priyanayanadehameghā has made offerings to many Buddhas, and her influence extends far and wide.

Volume Seventy: A single ray of light was emitted from the hair-tuft by Samantabhadra, and Sudhana attained the purity of the three spheres. Through their questions and answers, he clearly and sequentially attended upon many honored ones; having encountered virtuous friends over distant kalpas, his understanding was opened and expanded.

Volume Seventy-One. In this seventy-first volume, "Tranquility" and "Guarding the City" open the gates of liberation for Sudhana; each and every one is profound, vast, and inconceivable, with successive layers all synthesizing the past and the present.
Fascicle Seventy-two. The Friend Who Causes the Tree-Flowers to Bloom speaks the name of liberation.
The Great Joyous Radiance Wheel-Turning King establishes the site for the bestowal of the Dharma-gift.
The Night Goddess’s assembly recounts the ancient tale of the cultivation of the eyes.
In the seventy-third fascicle, the Dharma Gate of Great Vows, Sudhana beholds the city of Suprabha.
When the Father King beheld the Buddha, the Crown Prince was spared from the crime of execution.
Fascicle Seventy-four: The Seventh in this Fascicle is the Spirit of Wondrous Virtue, who presides over the treasury of the ten modes of rebirth.
Within the womb of Mother Māyā, the wonders of three thousand supernatural transformations were manifested.

In the seventy-fifth fascicle, Sudhana visits the deity Guṇavatī, who instructs him on the admonitions for seeking spiritual friends, recounts the past event of meeting the Buddha as his father-in-law, and reveals the superior conditions for practicing vows in concert.
Volume Seventy-Six, Volume Seventy-Six: Māyā serves as the model for the mothers of all Buddhas; may she abide in the standards of speech and conduct.
Her spiritual friends, such as Viśvāmitra and Prabhāsa, are all gathered through the conditions that give rise to entry into meditative concentration.
Volume Seventy-Seven. The seventy-seventh volume concerns the instructions for the youth and maiden on the hundredfold dharmas for befriending Sudhana.
Maitreya regards them with compassionate mindfulness and, through verses of praise, leads them back to their original teacher.
In the seventy-eighth fascicle, Sudhana encounters the opportunity and offers his words, while Maitreya, endowed with perfect virtue, is able to receive him.
The scripture comprises more than three hundred sections, manifesting the excellence of the bodhicitta and its loftiness of merit.

Volume Seventy-nine. Volume seventy-nine: Sudhana enters the gate of the pavilion and beholds the events of infinite kalpas across dust-mote worlds; through dharma-discourse, parables, and questions and answers, he withdraws from his seat, vowing that he shall attain the fruit of the Way and renew his aspiration.

Volume Eighty: Mañjuśrī extends his hand as if holding [the youth], and Sudhana attains the realization of the ultimate fruit; Samantabhadra touches his head with his hand and exhorts him with a verse: "Be careful not to harbor doubts regarding this sutra."
The general meaning of each volume of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* has been briefly narrated. Completed on the eighteenth day of the second month in the year of Hai (the 7th year of Daiei).
Regarding the intent of this transcription:
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is the fundamental wheel of the Dharma throughout the entire dispensation; it directly reveals the inner realization of the Tathāgata.
Those who touch his ears but once will forever be liberated from the retributive suffering of birth and death.
The Layman Tongxuan was a patriarch of the Avataṃsaka school; because his preaching of the sutras accorded with the Buddha’s intent, golden light radiated from his mouth.
To speak of "that" and "this" is something that cannot exist for one who lacks faith.
Nevertheless, the general purport of these eighty fascicles is such that, as soon as one has squeezed the paper and ink within one's palms to their limit, it reveals the subtle and essential art.
I, Ken, have daily borne this upon my head, disregarding the lack of paper and ink, and have transcribed it with my poor hand.
May the Three Jewels and the assembly of the unseen world take pity and accept it.
Kuai Xian, Chapter Forty-seven.
